# The register rules: Nuada

The internet spells **Nuada** more ways than one, and only one of them is the name the sources wrote. This is the register's ruling — canonical, fallback, contested, and false, each in its proper place.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Nuada
- **Original script:** —
- **Pantheon:** Celtic
- **Convention:** the tradition’s own scholarly transliteration standard
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 279 of 437

## The Canonical Form

The tradition's record preserves this name in its romanized scholarly form: **Nuada** — no older script survives to transcribe, so the canonical content is the exactness of the spelling itself.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form the tradition’s convention demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *nuada* differs from the canonical **Nuada** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — the tradition’s standard — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Nuada**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## The Convention's Own History

Every tradition in this register has its own scholarly transliteration standard, built by its own specialists over decades or centuries, and the register follows each on its own terms: the tradition’s own standard. The principle that unifies them is the one the whole project stands on: a name is evidence, and evidence is not negotiable — not for keyboards, not for convenience, not for anyone.

## What the Address Bar Allows

IDNA 2008 permits the letters these restorations use — macrons, acutes, underdots, thorn, ogonek, the lot — and the DNS carries them as punycode (`xn--` labels). Two honest constraints remain. First, **registrar inventory**: the protocol permits a character; the registrar's stock decides whether the exact domain can be bought today. Second, **combined marks**: forms like *Apṓllōn* (acute stacked on a macron) are philologically ideal yet effectively untypeable on phones and unsupported across much of the registration system.

That is why the rulebook keeps a fallback hierarchy — full restoration first, then the circumflex when the source carries one, then the macron-only academic standard, then an attested variant, and only as a last resort the plain ASCII form. **Every step down the ladder is still defensible; nothing on the ladder is a wrong mark.** A fallback is a choice among attested forms. A false form is not on the ladder at all.

## Where the Name Stood First

Nuada is textual in Ireland — no inscription names him there — but his Gaulish cognate has one of the best-excavated cult sites in Roman Britain. At Lydney Park, Gloucestershire, overlooking the Severn estuary, a temple complex of the late third and fourth centuries CE was dedicated to Nodens: the Wheelers' excavations (1928–29, published 1932 with Tolkien's philological appendix) uncovered mosaic floors, inscribed slabs reading DEVO NODENTI and D M NODONTI ('to the god Mars Nodens'), bronze dog figurines, a fisherman plaque, and pins and bracelets left as votives — the material of a healing-and-hunting cult. The famous curse tablet of Silvianus, asking Nodens to withhold health from whoever stole his ring until it was returned 'to the temple of Nodens', was found on the site; a gold ring inscribed SENICIANE VIVAS IN DEO, plausibly the very ring, surfaced at Silchester. On the Irish side, the texts are the evidence: the Second Battle of Mag Tuired survives in the sixteenth-century British Library Harley MS 5280, the First Battle in a single late vellum copy edited by Fraser, and the Lebor Gabála in its medieval recensions. The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Verdict

The register rules for **Nuada**, and the ruling is checkable: every mark sourced, every violation stated, every borderline form given its honest standing. *nuada* carries the name freely — it differs only in display, and the register says so without reservation. Anything else in circulation has its origin and its failure recorded above. That is the whole of the law on this name — and the temple at [/nuada/](/nuada/) enforces it.

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 8 cited sources — Lebor Gabála Érenn (The Book of Invasions of Ireland), ed. and trans. R. A. S. Macalister, Irish Texts Society — the arrival, the First Battle, the silver arm, Miach's healing, and the kingship of Bres, Cath Maige Tuired (The Second Battle of Mag Tuired), ed. and trans. Elizabeth A. Gray, Irish Texts Society 52 (1982) — Lugh's coming to Tara and Nuada's death at Balor's hand, J. Fraser, 'The First Battle of Moytura', Ériu 8 (1916) — the sole-copy text of the battle against the Fir Bolg and Sreng's stroke.
